items.originalTitle: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
items.author: Andrew Pulver
items.title: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
items.summary: Was it all a dream? Has Bond been in hiding? Or will Robert Pattinson simply report to HR on his first day? Russell T Davies, David Hare and more give their takes “James Bond will return,” says the closing title on No Time to Die, the most recent James Bond film and the final one to star Daniel Craig. It is just as well: Bond has to all appearances been vaporised by sea-launched missiles, having been infected by nanobots programmed to attack his nearest and dearest at the slightest touch. No one would believe that one of the world’s most successful film series would come to such an abrupt halt, but no doubt a little reassurance helped. Nevertheless, the first order of business for scriptwriter Steven Knight and director Denis Villeneuve will be dealing with it: how to revive and re-energise a character at the heart of the action. Speculation on their best way forward has been rife, and previous examples are not hard to find. Sherlock Holmes was killed off by Arthur Conan Doyle by fighting his arch enemy Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls in the story The Final Problem, only to resuscitate him a decade later with The Adventure of the Empty House. Superman is apparently killed at the end of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice, but resurrected in Justice League for the fight against Steppenwolf. Arguably the most enduring pop-culture return is Bobby Ewing’s famous shower scene in the TV show Dallas in 1986, which attempted to ensure continuity by suggesting Ewing’s death was his wife’s dream. And even Ian Fleming toyed with killing off Bond, with a climactic poison scene at the end of his 1957 novel From Russia with Love, and leaving him amnesiac and vulnerable to Soviet attack at the finish of You Only Live Twice, the last Bond novel published in Fleming’s lifetime.

items.title: Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages
items.summary: After a humiliating NBA finals defeat, the 22-year-old has returned with a vengeance – and the Spurs look like contenders again It wouldn’t be exactly right to say Victor Wembanyama didn’t miss a beat after a disastrous NBA finals in June that left him and his San Antonio Spurs defeated, memed and embarrassed. In the Spurs’ first game this season, against an Oklahoma City Thunder team since decimated by injuries, Wemby went an appalling 1-for-13 from the field. Ten of his 12 points came via free throws. After getting blocked by Aday Mara, the Thunder’s 7ft 3in offseason pickup clearly designed to counter the even more towering Wembanyama, he leaned over his knees and muttered furiously to himself as if trying to exorcise an intrusive thought. It brought to mind an image from the NBA finals a few months earlier: Wemby on the floor after being fouled by the Knicks’ Mitchell Robinson, crowing, “I’m in your head!” The Spurs went on to blow a 29-point lead , lose the game and the finals. Now Wemby seemed too preoccupied with the issues within his own dome to worry about wreaking havoc in anybody else’s. Game two saw Wembanyama elect to lay the ball up instead of dunking it in the dying seconds of a close tilt with the Houston Rockets, which the springy Amen Thompson blocked spectacularly . Not a great start, and in a league whose narratives calcify long before sample sizes reach an adequate scale, it allowed for whispers that the Spurs were in trouble. But you could say Wembanyama has not missed a beat since then . After beginning the season 0-2, the Spurs are now 13-3, with 12 of those wins coming in a row before a loss to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday. San Antonio’s basketball hasn’t been as seamless as those numbers suggest – the starting lineup includes three guards, leaving the offense a bit clunky and wanting for three-point shooting. It also includes Wembanyama, which papers over pretty much every possible problem.

items.title: Rob Sand shuts down any talk of 2028
items.summary: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand isn’t indulging any consideration of him as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. Sand, who cemented himself as a rising star in the party by flipping the governor’s seat in Iowa with a commanding 11-point victory, said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum that he’s unlikely to ever consider running for president. “Are you completely taking 2028 off the table?” POLITICO’s Adam Wren asked Sand. “Yes,” he replied. When asked if he would ever consider running for president, Sand curtly replied, “Doubt it.” Sand offered a tongue-in-cheek rebuttal to the suggestion that he could position himself as an influential voice and a power broker in the national conversation ahead of the next election. “Ooh, that sounds exciting,” Sand quipped sarcastically before adding, “I expect to be a governor in 2027 and in 2028.” Sand also declined to weigh in on his preference for who Democrats should nominate in the presidential primaries. Asked to choose between Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — all of whom campaigned for Democrats in Iowa in the midterms — Sand refused to take the bait. “We have forever to go on all of this,” he said. “The people who want to do that, they're going to get in the race. They're going to do things. They're going to say things. We'll learn a lot more. Then we'll have a clear opinion about who should be doing what.” Sand reiterated that he intends to keep Iowa’s Democratic caucuses as the first nominating contest on the calendar despite the Democratic Party removing Iowa from its early state lineup and encouraged Democratic presidential candidates to continue the tradition of visiting Iowa’s state fair next year. “I'm pretty confident that we'll figure something out that means we're following Iowa law, and they're going to be able to do that,” he said.

items.originalTitle: In Elsinore, a Radiant Andrew Scott Finds Life in a Play About Death
items.author: Stephanie Zacharek
items.title: In Elsinore, a Radiant Andrew Scott Finds Life in a Play About Death
items.summary: Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore —Courtesy of Focus Features Contracting HIV is no longer a death sentence. But before the current medications and treatments emerged, the AIDS crisis of the 1980s and 1990s touched almost everyone, gay or straight, whether you wanted to admit it or not. Friends of friends, acquaintances or associates who brightened your day, or, worst of all, a loved one: people you cherished could wither and disappear in practically a heartbeat. The performing arts were hit especially hard, and there’s no way to reckon with the unfulfilled potential of the many gifted individuals who died prematurely. If you’d forgotten what it was like to live with the specter of AIDS, or if you weren’t alive at the time, Simon Stone’s biographical drama Elsinore —in which Andrew Scott stars as actor Ian Charleson, who landed the role of a lifetime just as he was becoming seriously ill with AIDS—brings back the mood of the time, not in a maudlin way but a bittersweet one. The Scottish-born Charleson had become famous for his starring role in 1981’s Chariots of Fire , a film millions saw and, not long after it won a slew of Oscars, promptly forgot. As Elsinore opens, circa 1989, we see Scott as Charleson looking listless in his nicely appointed London flat. The roles haven’t been pouring in, and when his agent reminds him of his Chariots success, he grumbles, “All they remember is the theme music.” Then Charleson gets news that may as well be a gift from the gods. While playing Hamlet in a 1989 National Theatre production, Daniel Day-Lewis had walked off the stage abruptly, never to return. The play’s director, Richard Eyre (played by Johnny Flynn , in a performance of such warmth it feels lit from within), wants Charleson to take over the role. The job is everything he’d longed for. But just as he’s beginning to feel that his career could once again soar, he notices a small lesion on his temple, a marker of the illness that so many of his friends and colleagues—among them filmmaker and gay rights activist Derek Jarman, played by David Dawson—are already fighting. Scott and Coleman in Elsinore —Courtesy of Focus Features How Charleson perseveres in making the role of Hamlet his own—often despite the protestations of the AIDS specialist who’s treating him, Olivia Colman’s Margaret Johnson—is Elsinore ’s elegiac triumph. The script, by Stephen Beresford (writer of the 2014 historical comedy Pride ), never veers into mawkishness, nor does it downplay the stark reality of Charleson’s debilitations. And while it’s understandable that he’d want to hide his illness for professional reasons, even from his fellow Hamlet performers, Charleson’s secretiveness rankles some of his friends, including Jarman, who believes transparency about AIDS is the only way to gain the public attention. Scott’s performance is both elegant and feral, and it cuts to the heart of some of the era’s political complexities. Charleson was 40 when he played Hamlet; he pulled off a highly acclaimed six-week run and died eight weeks later. Scott plays Charleson with a grand hedgehog spikiness. If he has the energy to fight for only one cause, he’ll choose the grandeur of art. Both down to earth and crabbily noble, he won’t let anyone tell him what to do, not even Colman’s Johnson. “Nobody ever leaves Hamlet thinking, ‘Gosh, what a short night of light entertainment!’” she tells Charleson, and she’s not wrong about the demands of the role. The beautiful paradox of Elsinore is that a play about death should be the thing that fills an actor’s last days with so much life. We can see Charleson outrunning his fate for as long as he can. He grouses at his friends, and at Johnson—basically at anyone who’d dare tell him he’s doing it all wrong. Like the character he’s playing onstage, Scott’s Charleson is a stubborn, unruly prince, radiant with life even as it’s being drained out of him. It’s in his most unlikable moments that we love him the most.

items.originalTitle: Elsinore and the Remarkable True Story of a Dying Actor’s Triumph as Hamlet
items.author: JP Mangalindan
items.title: Elsinore and the Remarkable True Story of a Dying Actor’s Triumph as Hamlet
items.summary: Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore —Courtesy of Focus Features On the evening of Nov. 13, 1989, Ian Charleson walked onto the Olivier stage at London’s National Theatre to play Hamlet for the last time. He was 40 years old and dying of AIDS, though few of the 1,150 or so people watching from the dark knew it. The illness had puffed the skin around his eyes and affected his throat and chest, but the change in his face had been explained away as sinus surgery. The Olivier is the largest of the National's three auditoriums, its seats curving in a wide arc around the stage. It is a notoriously hard room to play to, one that tempts actors to force their voices. Charleson did not. Ian McKellen, who was there that night, later wrote of the younger actor delivering Hamlet's great speeches as one person talks to another, in a voice that stayed firm, making the huge auditorium feel uncharacteristically intimate. When Hamlet wished that his own flesh would melt away, Charleson's hands came up to shield his face, and they were thin and drained of color. At the end of nearly four hours, the audience rose to him. He never appeared onstage again. Elsinore , in theaters beginning on Nov. 20, builds up to that climactic night. Stephen Beresford, the screenwriter of Pride , wrote the film, which follows Charleson through his last months. During that time, the actor best known for playing the Scottish sprinter Eric Liddell in the 1981 Olympic drama Chariots of Fire took on Hamlet, the grieving Danish prince and the longest role Shakespeare wrote, just as his body was beginning to fail him. Andrew Scott, who plays Charleson with wit and coiled ferocity, leads a cast that includes Olivia Colman as Margaret Johnson, the physician who treated him; Billie Piper as Patsy Pollock, the casting director and friend who cared for him; and Johnny Flynn as Richard Eyre, the director who gave him the part. The film moves between the ward at the Royal Free Hospital in north London, where Charleson was a patient, and the rehearsal rooms of the National, where he was a prince, and carries him from the offer of the part, through the arguments over whether he should take it, to the ovation on his last night. Beneath the backstage detail and the Shakespeare, Elsinore hinges on the moment when a man who has been told how he will die decides how he will live until then, and on what that decision asked of those who loved him. Director Simon Stone, whose stage work includes a production of Hamlet , says the people who loved Charleson were caught between protecting him and letting him choose.. "There's this terrible tension between wanting to preserve someone's life and also letting them determine the way that their own life is going to be lived," he tells TIME. "At the end of the day it was Ian's choice, and Ian's choice was an extraordinary gift, ultimately, for so many audience members that got to see him play that part." The actor his friends remember Andrew Scott and Joe Locke in Elsinore —Courtesy of Focus Features Charleson was born in Edinburgh in 1949. His father was a printer. Local theater had the boy on stage by the time he was 8, and both his church and his school choir counted him among their sopranos. He reached the Royal High School and the University of Edinburgh on scholarships, enrolled to study architecture, and left as an actor. He trained at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art and, by the end of the 1970s, had worked his way to the National and the Royal Shakespeare Company. Then came Chariots of Fire and Liddell. A devout Christian, the real-life athlete would not race on a Sunday, so at the 1924 Olympics he gave up his best event, the 100 meters, and won gold in the 400 instead. The film, known for its slow-motion sprint along a beach and its iconic synthesizer theme, was named Best Picture at the 1982 Academy Awards, and so, a year later, was Gandhi , with Charleson as the clergyman Charlie Andrews. His best work, though, was in the theater, much of it at the National, where Eyre directed him as Sky Masterson in a celebrated Guys and Dolls in 1982, and where, in 1988, he played Brick in Tennessee Williams' Cat on a Hot Tin Roof . Beresford interviewed Charleson's friends and colleagues and found that grief had not made them solemn. "Because he was an actor, his friends are actors, and actors have a strong sense of humor," he says. "So I got a lot of stories from them that were very funny, and that really helped me to find his voice." Charleson, he adds, "really always saw the joke, both in life and in a play." Scott heard the same from everyone he asked. "He was really deeply loved, Ian, by anyone who encountered him, and he was enormously fun," he says. "That, to me, was the key to him, that he was somebody who was very light in spirit. I think he was troubled, of course, as you would be by what he was going through, but I think he was enormously courageous, and he was very witty and funny, and he knew how to have fun. As an attribute in a human being, to be fun-loving is sort of underestimated sometimes." But even after his success on screen and stage, one role still felt unfinished: Hamlet. Charleson was 25 when the Cambridge Theatre Company took him on tour in the part, and he came home unhappy with what he had done. In 1988, during the run of Cat on a Hot Tin Roof , he told Eyre across a canteen table at the National that he wanted a run at Shakespeare's great parts. Hamlet is the meatiest of them all. Shakespeare set the play in the Danish castle of Elsinore, where a prince learns from his father's ghost that his uncle, now king and married to his mother, is the murderer. Told to take revenge, Hamlet spends most of the play failing to, feigning madness and asking, in the soliloquy that begins "To be, or not to be," whether life is worth going on with. By the end, nearly everyone at Elsinore is dead, Hamlet among them. "It is the actor's Everest," Beresford says of the role. And it is, he adds, the "ultimate play about life and death, and I think, faced with his own mortality, he saw an opportunity to express some of that, maybe." Charleson's Hamlet has long been remembered as the performance of a dying man. His friends, and the film that follows them, remember a quick, funny, unsatisfied actor who was offered the part he most wanted at the worst possible moment, and took it. An offer made out of friendship Johnny Flynn as Richard Eyre with Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson —Courtesy of Focus Features Eyre's Hamlet opened at the Olivier in March 1989 with Daniel Day-Lewis as the prince and Judi Dench as his mother. Several months into the play’s run, on the night of Sept. 5, during the scene in which Hamlet meets his father's ghost, Day-Lewis walked off in distress and did not come back. Day-Lewis was 15 when he lost his father, Cecil Day-Lewis, a poet, and he has said the scene confronted him with that memory. He has not acted on stage since. His understudy, Jeremy Northam, finished the performance that evening. The role that had brought one actor too close to a death would pass to another facing his own. The walkout was sudden, but Day-Lewis had already been due to leave the production. Three months earlier, Eyre’s diaries record, the actor had said he would leave before the run ended. Eyre, who had become the National’s director the year before, offered the part to Charleson in August, while Day-Lewis was still playing it, and his diary says he did so on feeling more than pragmatism and judgment. Charleson was set to take over the role on Oct. 9. Charleson had tested positive for HIV in 1986, and by 1989 his health was failing. The gravity of his illness was clear to Eyre, though the nearness of the end was not. Charleson wondered aloud to Eyre whether an actor who looked as he did could really play Hamlet. He would recover, Eyre told him, and Charleson answered that they had to stay hopeful. To Hilton McRae, an actor and a friend since their student days in Edinburgh, he put it as a joke: the audience would greet his first entrance by leafing through their programs simply to find out who he was. Eyre made the casting decision out of friendship, and he has stood by it. He had a healthy, capable actor already playing the part, and most people around him thought the choice reckless. By the middle of September, Eyre's diary records, word had reached him that the Sunday Mirror was asking whether Charleson had AIDS and would be well enough to open the following month. Reporters came to Charleson's door in west London, and at the National, a vandal defaced his photograph with a cross. The film compresses these events: on screen, the offer comes only after Day-Lewis has gone. Flynn plays Eyre as steady and generous; the real Eyre was less composed at the time. Stone never met Charleson, but he heard enough stories about him to guess how the argument was won. "He was an incredibly charming, gregarious, and very convincing person, and I imagine that when he wanted something, he was going to get it," Stone says. Letting an actor that weak play Hamlet was, he adds, a "terrifying thing," though Stone is thankful it happened all the same: by every account, the people in the room watched one of the great performances of their lives. The people who held him up Billie Piper as Patsy Pollock with Andrew Scott —Courtesy of Focus Features In 1989, the combination drug therapies that would make HIV treatable were still years away. The one licensed drug, AZT, bought little time, and the stigma around the disease reached all the way into law: Section 28, passed by Margaret Thatcher's government in 1988, barred local authorities from what it termed promoting homosexuality. Charleson was open with his friends about being gay but had never come out publicly, and he kept his illness private as well. Derek Jarman chose otherwise. The filmmaker who gave Charleson one of his first screen roles, in the 1978 punk film Jubilee , went public about his own HIV diagnosis within weeks of receiving it in December 1986, and his activism and visibility became central to his work. Charleson's work, for as long as he could still do it, required him to seem well. Elsinore pits the two against each other: David Dawson plays Jarman, and the two men argue on screen over what a gay artist owes the public during an epidemic. Charleson's doctor, Johnson, was a lung specialist early in her career, and the HIV service at the Royal Free was hers to build. His name meant nothing to her when he became her patient. She ended up dealing with the National as well: more than once, when Charleson felt too ill to telephone Eyre himself, she made the call for him. Beresford sought out the real Johnson and asked about Hamlet. "I said to her, 'I understand you had reservations about Ian playing Hamlet,' and she said, 'Yes, well, I was right,'" he says. "And I said, 'What makes you say that?' And she says, 'Well, he's dead.'" In that answer, Beresford heard a deadpan humor and a pragmatism, an "absolute truth-teller element," and the doctor and her patient became one of the film's central relationships. On screen, Colman's Johnson at first does not want him playing Hamlet. Charleson's reason for pressing on, as Stone quotes it: "I'd rather die of Hamlet than AIDS." Beresford built their scenes on two people who look like opposites, the scientist and the artist, and turn out to share more than either expects. "When they start to see that in each other, I think that's what changes her mind," he says. "I suppose in a way it's Shakespeare that changes her mind, because that's what he uses to get to her finally." The friends closest to Charleson were no more united than his doctor and his director. Sean Mathias, the theater director, played on screen by Matthew Beard, thought he should not do it. Pollock, a casting director, thought he should, and then made it possible. Stone calls her the person Charleson depended on most. "She sacrificed huge amounts of time and energy to look after Ian in his dying weeks, especially when he was playing Hamlet," he says. "Otherwise, it would have been a very lonely time for Ian." The Hamlet company was not told at first what was really wrong with him. Within weeks, Charleson told them the truth himself, at a meeting of the full cast, and asked them to keep it among themselves. The meeting went much the way Elsinore stages it, and the company closed around him afterward with their support. Imagining a lost performance Olivia Colman as Dr. Margaret Johnson —Courtesy of Focus Features Beresford wrote Elsinore for Scott, who had acted in his film Pride and his solo play Three Kings and who joined the film as a producer as well as its lead. Scott gives the credit back to Beresford. "It was all really there, so much, on the page," he says. "Stephen did exhaustive research. He spoke to so many people in Ian's life, so I used Stephen's screenplay and Stephen himself as the basis." The script, he adds, was "always so funny," and the Charleson in it was "ferocious at times." What the script could not exactly recreate was Charleson's performance as Hamlet. Scott had played the role himself, roughly 150 times on the London stage in 2017, to praise for his conversational and quiet rendition, and those who saw Charleson remember the same quality in him. The Gertrude in the 2017 production, Juliet Stevenson, was a friend of Charleson's from the Royal Shakespeare Company; in Elsinore she plays Sylvia Syms, the Gertrude of his run. The Hamlet in Elsinore is not a reprise, though. In 2017 Scott gave the lines more room to breathe; as Charleson he plays them tighter, a different man's Hamlet. He could not copy the original, either: Scott had nothing to watch. "You use the biggest thing that you have as a tool as an actor, which is your imagination," he says. Stone filled the theater with about 200 supporting artists and let him play to a house. "When you go out in front of an audience, you have to be prepared to be inventive just on the day," Scott says. "You perform it, in some ways, with the atmosphere that's in the room." He was also conscious of what the soliloquy is: the "greatest speech about what happens after we die. That's of course what Ian was going to be going through within a matter of weeks after delivering that famous speech." The filmmakers approached Elsinore like a sports film, fitting for the man who played Liddell: Charleson's rehearsals are its training scenes, and they gather momentum as they go, each one a test of whether the body will hold until the big day. Scott's own preparation was physical, too. He is Irish, and for the part he wore blue contact lenses, had his hair recolored and worked with a dialect coach on what he calls Charleson's "very particular way of talking," a soft Edinburgh lilt in the voice of a gifted tenor. The shoot ran from early January 2026 into that February, and, as on many films, the scenes were shot out of sequence, so the illness could not play out as it would in life, one day at a time. "I had to sometimes be very well and unwell numerous times within a day," Scott says. Stone and his cinematographer kept the camera off the tripod and often close to Scott's face, and let the buildings around him loom. He wanted the National to feel, he says, "almost like it is the castle of Elsinore," where Shakespeare set the play. The theater and the Royal Free are, he points out, the same kind of place, vast concrete structures built by a Britain that, in the decades after the war, spent public money on the arts and on health care alike: "temples to art and life." When Stone reflects on how Scott surprised him on set, the filmmaker cites an especially intimate scene.. Charleson, in his hospital bed, is waiting for his parents, who are about to learn in one visit that their son is gay and that he has AIDS. He pulls his cardigan across a lesion. He fixes his hair. He tries out a smile. "That was all because I didn't say cut," Stone says. "I just let it keep rolling, and he kept playing the scene, and I just kept not cutting because it kept being more beautiful, and then eventually I had to cut, because he would have gone on forever." What he saw was a "terror in his eyes, and this little boy that he becomes in that moment." Scott, asked about that scene, credits the people in the room with him: Georgie Glen and Peter Mullan as his parents, and a director he calls "very sensitive." "It's his lowest moment," he says. "Sometimes, I think that stuff is very physical, and so you just let your imagination take over." What he left behind Scott as Charleson, preparing to play Hamlet —Courtesy of Focus Features Charleson's run began on Oct. 9, 1989. Through Nov. 13, he played every performance his body allowed, and told Eyre he was sorry for the ones he missed; an actor who took the wage, he believed, owed the work. Paul Jesson, who played Hamlet's friend Horatio, often held him upright onstage, and by the last scenes of an evening, when Hamlet duels and dies, the sword had grown almost too heavy for him. Syms, who had replaced Dench as Gertrude, drove him home afterward, and he was asleep in the car before it reached his door. On Nov. 12, the day before what proved his last performance, the Sunday Times gave its critic John Peter a full page, and he filled it with praise for the intelligence and force of Charleson's Hamlet. The next night was his last. Eyre has written that the performance seemed the product of a whole life's preparation. The house stood, and Charleson faced it exhausted, as if the applause itself were hard to withstand; backstage he kept hold of the champagne a critic had given him while the congratulations went on. His strength held until he got home. The next day, McKellen accepted the Evening Standard’s best actor award, one of London’s major theater prizes, for playing Iago in the Royal Shakespeare Company’s Othello. He told the room the real best actor of the year was Charleson, whose Hamlet he had seen the night before. In the eight weeks he had left, Charleson talked about Hamlet with the friends who visited and kept a paperback of the play within reach of his bed. He put in an order for painting supplies, too, and laughed about the canvases he had left half done. He died at home in London on Jan. 6, 1990, of septicemia, a complication of AIDS, on the day his family flew down to be with him. His agent announced AIDS as the cause and said Charleson had wanted it known. McRae, his friend who has a small part in the film, has disputed that: by his account, family and friends decided the morning after his death what to tell the press. Charleson is believed to be the first British star whose death from AIDS was made public. Within the year, his name was on a prize for young actors in classical parts, set up by Peter and the Sunday Times with the National. Johnson's clinic at the Royal Free has carried his name since 1992: the Ian Charleson Day Centre. When Elsinore shows the National saluting him in its traditional way, with actors in the building hammering on their dressing-room windows, some of the faces at the glass belong to past real-life winners of the prize. Stone has his own way of putting what Charleson left behind. "We are only the impact we have on the people around us," he says. In making the film, Scott came to know Charleson's friends and family, and those connections left their mark. "I love the fact that I have a relationship with them," he says. What he heard from them was "how Ian was supported by members of my profession": a Horatio who often held Charleson upright onstage, a Gertrude who drove him home, a company that stood by him. "I've always been very happy to be an actor," Scott adds. "But I feel very proud of my profession when looking at this story." No recording of Charleson's Hamlet is known to exist. It survives in a diary, a Sunday review, a tribute written in grief, and the memories of the actors who shared the stage with him, and every year, there are fewer of them to ask. Charleson's own account is shorter, and it fits on a card. Eyre still keeps it. It came to him from the Royal Free shortly before Christmas in 1989, in the last weeks Charleson had; it says the part had thrilled him, for the short time he could play it, and that he hoped he had not dreamed it. "One day when I'm better I'd love to attempt Hamlet again," he wrote. He had played the title role in Hamlet at 25 and again at 40. He did not get a third go at it. What exists instead is Elsinore , in which Scott walks out, as Charleson did, before a rapt house watching from the dark, and lets Hamlet breathe again.

items.originalTitle: Massachusetts gov says Dems want ‘a uniter and a fighter’ for 2028
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: Massachusetts gov says Dems want ‘a uniter and a fighter’ for 2028
items.summary: Democrats want fighters. Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey believes they want healers, too. Healey, a Democrat who easily won a second term in the deep-blue state earlier this month, told POLITICO on Thursday that she’d like to see her party’s next presidential nominee show “decency” and “humanity.” “It’s really important that we have leaders who genuinely see people, understand their situation. If you don't see people, if you don't understand people, you're never going to be able to deliver for them,” Healey said during an interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “Having leaders who have that, and who have a strong moral compass, I think that's really important,” she told POLITICO’s Adam Wren. Healey suggested the midterms offered a “resetting” as the nation moves toward a post-Donald Trump era. Pressed on whether it’s more important for Democrats to nominate a fighter or a healer, Healey — who burnished her national profile as a hard-charging state attorney general who sued the first Trump administration dozens of times and urged Democrats to more aggressively oppose his second — insisted good leaders can do both. “You can be a uniter and a fighter; you can be a fighter and a healer,” she said. It’s a debate that’s already driving the earliest stages of Democrats’ shadow 2028 primary as the party’s rising stars try to discern whether voters who powered their midterm wave want a brawler or a uniter after candidates of both stripes won difficult races. Healey ruled out a 2028 presidential bid of her own on Thursday. And she deflected when asked whether Democrats should nominate a governor. But the Massachusetts governor, who has close relationships with several likely contenders and routinely hits the campaign trail for Democrats in the early primary state of New Hampshire, could play a role in shaping the primary.

items.originalTitle: Keisha Lance Bottoms says Democrats better spend big on the South
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms says Democrats better spend big on the South
items.summary: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said the midterm election results “have spoken for themselves” in showing the need for the Democratic Party to invest more in the South. “I would hope that in two years, we're not having to beg and borrow to be able to run successful campaigns,” Bottoms said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. Democrats had a historically strong cycle in Georgia this year: Bottoms became the first Democrat to win her state’s governorship in more than a quarter-century, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection handily, and the party flipped the state House for the first time in more than two decades. But it wasn’t just Georgia. Democrats also won Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, three states that have long been out of reach for the party, and just missed in Louisiana. “The numbers have been there for Democrats to flip that seat in Mississippi for a while, but the investment has not been there,” Bottoms said. She said that her campaign was a lean operation, particularly in contrast to her GOP opponent’s. Rick Jackson spent nearly $200 million of his own money on his campaign. “During the primary it was the shoestring, dental floss campaign, we were holding it together with every single thing that we had because we weren't getting in the resources and some people have written Georgia off,” she said. “But also even when those resources come from our friends nationally: Trust us. Nobody knows their community, nobody knows their electorate better than the people who are living and breathing it every single day.” Bottoms made history as the first-ever Black woman ever elected governor to in the U.S. earlier this month. But on her campaign trail, she did not focus on the historic nature of her candidacy. “I wake up as a Black woman every day,” she said. “So it was not something that I felt compelled to talk about, it was never top of mind, so it was not even a conscious decision for me not to talk about it. I just didn’t think about it.” She said she instead focused on voters’ cost of living concerns that dominated the cycle. “For me, it was about focusing on the issues. I can't hide, and don't want to hide, that I'm a Black woman,” she said. “To the extent that the conversations were organic with me as a mother or as a woman or whatever the case may have been, then it was a part of the discussion. But I can tell you, as I moved around the state of Georgia, people were focused on, ‘what are you gonna do about this cost of living? How are you going to make my life better?’”
